Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
List the radiographs and advanced imaging studies necessary for a complete evaluation of
young adults with hip pain.
Describe radiographic measurements that can be used to identify or classify common hip
conditions, such as femoroacetabular impingement, acetabular dysplasia, and osteonecrosis
of the hip.
Outline key imaging findings in common conditions of the young adult hip.

Obtaining a correct diagnosis is a challenge; subtle symptoms may go unrecognized,
predisposing the patient to pain and/or joint degeneration. Imaging of the hip and pelvis
is vital to diagnostic workup and has evolved considerably because of new concepts in
hip morphology and biomechanics and the increasing number of arthroscopic hip
procedures performed. Radiography, MRI, CT, and ultrasonography are the key imaging
modalities for evaluation of the hip and pelvis. Specific considerations are important in
evaluating a painful hip joint in patients who may have femoroacetabular impingement
(FAI), labral tears, developmental dysplasia of the hip, osteoarthritis, osteonecrosis,
ischiofemoral impingement, or snapping hip.
Radiography
The goals of radiography are to identify structural anatomy and pathoanatomy, degenerative
changes, and femoroacetabular joint congruency.
Weight-bearing radiographs allow for analysis of the impact of body weight and upright
alignment on hip and pelvic anatomy.
The main radiographic views include AP pelvis and lateral views (Resource 1).
AP Pelvis Radiographs
Useful to assess femoroacetabular coverage, arthritis, and fractures
Osteoarthritis with a joint space less than 2.0 mm or a Tönnis grade higher than 2 is associated
with poorer hip arthroscopy outcomes1
Key measurements
Joint space
Normal is greater than 2 mm
Femoral neck-shaft angle
Normal ranges from 125° to 135°
Lateral center-edge angle (LCEA)
Normal ranges from 25° to 35°
Tönnis angle (acetabular index)
Normal is less than 13°
Femoro-epiphyseal acetabular roof (FEAR) index
Normal is less than 5°


AP Pelvis Radiographs
An AP pelvis radiograph identifies acetabular coverage of the femoral head, remaining
joint space, femoroacetabular congruency, femoral head sphericity, acetabular
inclination, femoroacetabular joint center, leg lengths, femoral head cysts, osteonecrotic
lesions, acetabular cysts, and fractures. This view is obtained with the patient bearing
weight and the x-ray beam centered between the superior border of the pubic
symphysis and a line connecting the anterior superior iliac spines. On supine AP pelvis
radiographs, internal rotation of the lower extremities by 15° maximizes the length of
the femoral neck. The center of the femoral head should be in line with or just medial to
the rim of the posterior wall. Symmetry should be assessed between the two
hemipelvises (eg, obturator foramen, iliac wing, teardrop), and the horizontal position of
the sacrum and coccyx relative to the pubic symphysis (Figure 1). More than 2 mm of
joint space narrowing indicates advanced disease and has been identified as a risk factor
for failed arthroscopic management.1 The two most common classifications to evaluate
the degree of osteoarthritis are the Tönnis grade and the Kellgren-Lawrence scale.
Tönnis grade
Grade 0: normal joint space; no arthritis changes.
Grade 1: slight narrowing of joint space, increasing subchondral sclerosis of the
acetabulum and/or femoral head, mild osteophyte formation
Grade 2: small cysts in the femoral head or acetabulum, moderate joint-space
narrowing, moderate loss of sphericity of the femoral head
Grade 3: large cysts in the femoral head or acetabulum, severe joint space
narrowing or obliteration, severe deformity of the femoral head
Kellgren-Lawrence scale
Grade 0: normal
Grade 1: doubtful narrowing of joint space and possible osteophytic lipping
Grade 2: definite osteophytes, definite narrowing of joint space
Grade 3: moderate multiple osteophytes, definite narrowing of joint space, some
sclerosis and possible deformity of bone contour
Grade 4: large osteophytes, marked narrowing of joint space, severe sclerosis, and
definite deformity of bone contour

Figure 1 AP pelvis radiograph obtained with the x-ray beam centered between the
superior border of the pubic symphysis and a line connecting the anterior superior iliac
spines, with 15° of internal rotation of the lower extremities if obtained with the patient
in the supine position. (Courtesy of Caitlin Chambers, MD, Minneapolis, MN.)
Several measurements can be determined on AP radiographs. Pelvic tilt is most
commonly assessed using the vertical distance between the superior pubic symphysis
and the center of the sacrococcygeal joint, or coccyx.2 This mean distance is 32.3 mm in
men and 47.3 mm in women. A distance of 1 to 3 cm from the tip of the coccyx to the
pubic symphysis suggests appropriate pelvic tilt.3 The femoral neck-shaft angle is formed
by the axis of the femoral shaft and a line drawn along the axis of the femoral neck,
passing through the center of the femur. Normal values range from 125° to 135°. In a
systematic review by Boese et al,4 the mean neck-shaft angle was 128.8° in healthy
adults. This angle is increased in coxa valga and decreased in coxa vara (Resource 1).
The LCEA (angle of Wiberg) assesses lateral coverage of the femoral head by the
acetabulum and is formed between a vertical line perpendicular to the transverse pelvic
axis (ie, inter-teardrop line) from the center of the femoral head and a second line drawn
from the center of the head to the lateral edge of the acetabular sourcil (Figure 2, A). An
SEND FEEDBACK

4/36

LCEA of 25° to 35° is considered normal.5 Increased values indicate focal or global over-
coverage (ie, pincer lesion or coxa profunda), and decreased values are observed with
under-coverage (acetabular dysplasia). The generally accepted cutoff value for
arthroscopy is a LCEA of 18° to 20° because of poor outcomes in hips with lower LCEAs,
which are observed in patients in more severe hip dysplasia.6 The inclination of the
weight-bearing surface of the acetabulum, or sourcil, is measured via the Tönnis angle
(acetabular index; Figure 2, B). This is the angle between a horizontal line at the level of
the medial edge of the sourcil and a line tangential to the medial and lateral edges of the
sourcil.7 The normal range is 13° or less, with higher values observed in patients with hip
dysplasia. The FEAR index is another measurement useful in patients with hip dysplasia.
It measures the angle between the central third of the femoral epiphyseal scar and the
acetabular sourcil8 (Figure 2, C). Angles diverging laterally are considered positive
values, and angles converging laterally are negative values. A more horizontally oriented
physeal scar results in more laterally directed joint force, which may increase instability
of the borderline dysplastic hip joint. A FEAR index of less than 5° is indicative of a stable
hip amenable to hip arthroscopy, whereas patients with a FEAR Index greater than 5° are
better suited for bony correction of dysplasia, such as a periacetabular osteotomy.9 The
Shenton line is a curved line drawn along the inferior border of the superior pubic ramus
and along the inferomedial border of the neck of the femur. This line should be smooth
and continuous.

Lateral Pelvis Radiographs
Several types of lateral hip radiographs can be obtained: cross-table lateral, Dunn and
modified Dunn, frog-lateral, and false-profile views.
They are useful to assess proximal femur anatomy, anterior and posterior joint spaces, and
the acetabular rim.
Key measurements
Alpha angle
Normal is less than 42° to 63°
Anterior femoral offset
Normal is 15 mm to 25 mm
Femoral offset ratio
Normal is 0.21 (± 0.03)
Anterior center edge angle (ACEA)
Normal is 20° to 45°

Lateral Pelvis Radiographs
Lateral radiographs of the pelvis help define the osseous anatomy of the proximal
aspect of the femur, the anterior and posterior joint spaces, and the acetabular rims.
Various lateral radiographs can be obtained.
For a cross-table lateral radiograph, the patient is placed supine, and the unaffected
limb is flexed at the hip to 90°. The affected limb is rotated internally 15°. The x-ray
beam is parallel to the table, angled at 45° and centered on the femoral head (Figure
3).

Figure 3 Cross-table lateral radiograph of a pelvis obtained with the x-ray beam
parallel to the table, angled 45°, and centered on the femoral head. The patient is in
the supine position, the unaffected limb is flexed 90°, and the affected limb is placed
in 15° of internal rotation. (Courtesy of Caitlin Chambers, MD, Minneapolis, MN.)
Dunn and modified Dunn radiographs are obtained at angles of 90° and 45° of hip
flexion, respectively. The patient is placed in the supine position, and the affected limb
is abducted by 20° with neutral rotation. The x-ray beam is between the anterior
superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis, perpendicular to the table (Figure 4).
This is the optimal radiographic view for assessment of anterolateral cam lesions. The
alpha angle, anterior femoral offset, and the femoral offset ratio can be evaluated on
these views. The alpha angle identifies loss of normal femoral head-neck offset and is
defined as the angle between the femoral neck axis and a line connecting the center
of the femoral head to the starting point of the superior femoral head asphericity
(Figure 5). The reported upper limit of normal ranges from 42° to 63°, with higher
values indicating a cam lesion.2,10 Anterior femoral head-neck offset (Figure 6) is
calculated on a lateral radiograph (cross-table or modified Dunn view) by drawing a
line bisecting the longitudinal axis of the femoral neck at its narrowest point, then
marking parallel lines tangent to the anterior border of the femoral neck and head.
The perpendicular distance between the lines at the anterior border of the femoral
head and neck is the anterior femoral head-neck offset (Figure 6). Normal values
range from 15 to 25 mm, with lower values observed in patients with a cam lesion.
The femoral offset ratio is the ratio between the anterior femoral head-neck offset

Figure 6 Lateral radiograph of a hip demonstrates measurement of anterior femoral
offset, which is the difference between the radius of the anterior femoral head and
the anterior femoral neck (normal, 15 mm to 25 mm). Line a indicates the center of
the femoral neck. Line b indicates the anterior femoral head. Line c indicates the
anterior femoral neck. Line d indicates the femoral head-neck offset. (Courtesy of
Caitlin Chambers, MD, Minneapolis, MN.)
Frog-lateral radiographs visualize the anterior femoral head-neck junction. With the
patient in the supine position, the knee is flexed on the affected side, and the hip is
abducted to 45° (Figure 7). Osteonecrosis is best visualized on this view and appears
as a radiolucent lesion with a sclerotic rim, classically in the superolateral aspect of
the femoral head. Osteonecrosis may demonstrate early collapse, as identified by the
crescent sign (Figure 8). The Ficat classification system is used for grading the severity
of osteonecrosis.
Ficat classification system
Stage 0: preclinical and preradiographic
Stage I: symptomatic but preradographic
Stage II: precollapse; sclerosis, cysts, diffuse porosis, crescent sign
Stage III: early femoral head collapse; head flattening, sequestrum formation
Stage IV: complete femoral head collapse, decreased joint space

Figure 8 Frog-lateral (A) and AP (B) radiographs of a hip demonstrate a crescent sign (arrows)

A false-profile radiograph identifies acetabular coverage anteriorly and posteriorly. The patient
stands with the affected hip against the cassette and the pelvis rotated 65°. The ipsilateral foot
remains parallel to the cassette, and the x-ray beam is centered on the femoral head,
perpendicular to the cassette (Figure 9). The ACEA (angle of Lequesne) can be measured on this
view. The ACEA is the angle between a vertical line drawn from the center of the femoral head
and another line drawn from the center of the femoral head to the anterior acetabular edge
(Figure 10). The normal ACEA range is 20° to 45°, and lower values indicate anterior under-
coverage, which can be observed in patients with acetabular dysplasia.

MRI/Magnetic Resonance Arthrography
MRI/magnetic resonance arthrography (MRA) help determine the integrity of the labral and
chondral surfaces and may alter surgical planning, depending on the amount of degeneration.
Radial and oblique axial MRIs can accurately locate and measure the size of the cam lesion to
help the surgeon preoperatively plan for femoral head-neck junction osteoplasty.
Newer MRI technologies may be useful for evaluating chondral integrity.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Main views include axial, coronal-oblique, sagittal, and radial.

MRI is useful for evaluating labral tears, chondral injury, edema, sclerosis, areas of
impingement, occult fractures, osteonecrosis, infection, and neoplasms.
Modified Kerboul method
Less than 190°: low risk
190° to 240°: moderate risk (50%)
Greater than 240°: high risk (near 100%)
Percentage of femoral head involvement observed on MRI to estimate risk of collapse
Less than 30%: low risk (5% collapse at 5 years)
30% to 50%: moderate risk (46% at 5 years)
>50%: high risk (83% or higher at 5 years)

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may be useful in delineating proximal femur and acetabulum deformities. The most
commonly used MRI is 1.5-tesla ; however, but the use of 3.0-T MRI is becoming more
common and allows for better definition of soft-tissue structures, potentially obviating
the need for arthrogram dye injection.12 MRI offers excellent diagnostic sensitivity with
regard to labral pathology (≥90%) but variable sensitivity (50% to 90%) with regard to
acetabular articular cartilage pathology.
MRI includes axial, coronal-oblique, sagittal, and radial views, which are obtained with
the patient in the supine position with the lower extremities in 15° of internal rotation to
control version of the femoral neck. MRIs are useful for evaluating chondral defects,
labral tears, bone edema, stress reaction, sclerosis, cystic changes in subchondral bone,
and localizing areas of bony impingement. MRI also can be useful for identifying occult
femoral head-neck fractures, osteonecrosis, septic joint or osteomyelitis, neoplasm, and
intra-articular pathology. The modified Kerboul method grades osteonecrosis to
estimate the risk for potential collapse by adding the arc of the femoral head necrosis on
midsagittal and midcoronal cuts (Figure 11). The percentage of femoral involvement
observed on MRI also can be used to estimate the risk of collapse.

midcoronal and midsagittal angle measurements, respectively. Using the modified
Kerboul method, the combined angular measurements of angle A and angle B may help
predict the risk of femoral head collapse from osteonecrosis. The risk of femoral head

Magnetic Resonance Arthrography
Contrast injected in the joint allows for improved visualization of chondrolabral integrity.

Magnetic Resonance Arthrography
MRA involves injection of dilute contrast solution under fluoroscopic or ultrasonographic
guidance. Articular cartilage is examined for shear injuries, flaps, or indentations.
Contrast traversing between the cartilage and subchondral bone and communicating

with the joint is consistent with a chondral tear. Similarly, full-thickness labral tears are
identified via contrast undercutting the acetabular labrum at the chondrolabral junction.
MRI Cartilage Mapping Techniques
Delayed gadolinium-enhanced MRI of cartilage and T2-weighted mapping aid in evaluating
cartilage and may help in predicting the success of various hip procedures.

MRI Cartilage Mapping Techniques
New MRI cartilage mapping techniques allow for assessment of cartilage biochemical
ultrastructure and health before the development of macroscopic defects. Delayed
gadolinium-enhanced MRI of cartilage delineates articular cartilage damage by
measuring the remaining glycosaminoglycan content and has prognostic value in
predicting patient responses to hip preservation osteotomy procedures.12 T2-weighted
mapping assesses the collagen and extracellular matrix components of cartilage.
Degraded cartilage has disrupted collagen and increased free water content, with higher
T2-weighted values than healthy cartilage.
Other Imaging Modalities
Ultrasonography allows for static and dynamic examination of the hip joint.
CT is particularly useful to assess osseous morphology.
Ultrasonography
Allows for dynamic evaluation of the hip joint

Ultrasonography

Ultrasonography allows for static and dynamic examination of the hip joint and soft-
tissue structures. Ultrasonography is not degraded by metallic artifact; therefore, it
proves especially useful in patients with prosthetic hips. Ultrasonography can be used to
confirm sources of mechanical complaints, such as snapping hip, or to visualize extra-
articular impingement dynamically.
Computed Tomography
Helpful in evaluating osseous structures, femoral head sphericity, occult fractures, and
acetabular and femoral version
Key measurements
Femoral version
Normal is 30° to 40° anteversion at birth and 8° to14° in adults
Acetabular version
Normal is 17° (± 6°) of anteversion

Computed Tomography
CT aids in the assessment of acetabular and femoral osseous morphology. Multidetector
CT affords improved spatial resolution and the ability to reformat in multiple planes
without additional radiation. Cystic changes within the bone and ossification of the
labrum can be delineated, and sphericity of the femoral head can be determined. The
alpha angle can be measure on sagittal oblique CT scans. Occult fractures can be
identified.
CT aids in measuring femoral and acetabular version, independent of patient
positioning. Femoral version is the angle between the long axis of the femoral neck and a
line parallel to the dorsal aspect of the femoral condyles on an axial CT scan (or axial
MRI). Mean femoral anteversion is between 30° and 40° at birth and between 8° and 14°
in adults, with men having slightly less femoral anteversion than women. Acetabular
version is the angle between a line connecting the anterior acetabular margin with the
posterior acetabular margin and a transverse reference line through the femoral head
centers. Normal values are 17° (± 6°) of anteversion.13 Acetabular retroversion may

create anterior over-coverage with impingement symptoms and classic chondrolabral
lesions similar to those with pincer-type FAI.
Occasionally, three-dimensional CT reconstruction images are used for preoperative
planning and to assess residual deformity in preparation for revision surgery. This can
provide an excellent model of the cam and pincer lesions in patients with FAI, which may
help with surgical planning of osteochondroplasty. The major disadvantage is radiation
exposure, because a CT scan of the hips or pelvis is associated with 5 to 7 mSv2.
Key Imaging Studies for Common Hip Pathology
Femoroacetabular Impingement
FAI is the abnormal contact between the proximal femur and acetabulum, leading to labral
damage and varying degrees of chondral injury.
Primary types are cam, pincer, and mixed types.
Cam impingement is caused by decreased femoral head-neck offset deformities of the
anterolateral head-neck junction.
Pincer impingement results from acetabular over-coverage and results in direct impaction of
the acetabular rim and femoral neck.
Cam Impingement
Results from decreased femoral head-neck offset of the anterolateral head-neck junction with
resultant osseous protuberance or pistol-grip deformity
Cam-type impingement also can arise secondary to other conditions, resulting in abnormal
shape of the femoral head, such as previous slipped capital femoral epiphysis, Legg-Calvé-
Perthes disease, or malunited femoral neck fractures.
Key radiographic findings
Decreased femoral head-neck offset
Anterior femoral head-neck offset less than 7.2 mm
Femoral offset ratio less than 0.17
Alpha angle greater than 50°


Cam Impingement
Cam impingement results from decreased femoral head-neck offset of the anterolateral
head-neck junction. Cam impingement is caused by reduction in offset of the femoral
head-neck junction, osseous protuberance, aspheric femoral head, previous slipped
capital femoral epiphysis, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, or malunited femoral neck
fractures. Several radiographic findings are observed in patients with cam impingement.
The decreased femoral head-neck offset can be observed as a pistol-grip deformity, in
which the femoral head-neck junction is no longer concave but flat, or even convex.
Large cam lesions can be observed on AP radiographs, whereas more subtle cam lesions
are best visualized on lateral radiographs of the hip (modified Dunn, Dunn, frog-lateral
views; Figure 12). Anterior femoral offset of less than 7.2 (± 0.7 mm), a femoral offset
ratio less than 0.17, and an alpha angle greater than 50° may be associated with cam-
type FAI.2
Figure 12 AP pelvis radiograph demonstrates a reduction in head and neck offset far
laterally (arrows). (Courtesy of Caitlin Chambers, MD, Minneapolis, MN.)

Secondary causes of cam-type impingement include previous malunited femoral neck
fracture, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease. These
conditions may result in deformed and aspheric femoral heads. In particular, Legg-Calvé-
Perthes disease is associated with coxa magna, coxa breva, a mushroom-shaped
aspheric femoral head, overriding greater trochanter, and acetabular dysplasia.
Pincer Impingement
Results from focal anterolateral acetabular over-coverage
Key radiographic findings
Crossover sign
LCEA greater than 35°
Low Tönnis angle (acetabular index)
Os acetabuli
Acetabular retroversion also creates anterolateral over-coverage and may result in symptoms
and chondrolabral injuries akin to those observed in patients with pincer-type FAI.
Global acetabular over-coverage may be associated with similar symptoms but may prove
challenging to manage surgically given its non-focal nature.
Acetabular protrusio
Coxa profunda

Pincer Impingement
Pincer impingement results from acetabular over-coverage and causes direct impaction
of the acetabular rim and femoral neck. Classic pincer-type FAI is caused by focal lateral
acetabular overhang. Radiographic findings consistent with a pincer lesion include a
crossover sign, low Tönnis angle (acetabular index), and LCEA greater than 35°.2 The
crossover sign is observed as the posterior acetabular rim (ilioischial line) crossing over
the anterior rim (iliopectineal line) on an AP pelvis radiograph (Figure 13, B). An os
acetabuli also can be observed in patients with pincer-type impingement and represents
an extension of the lateral acetabular rim from bony apposition or labral ossification
from repeated microtrauma.

With acetabular retroversion, loss of the normal acetabular anteversion occurs, resulting
in anterolateral acetabular over-coverage similar to that observed in patients with

Global acetabular over-coverage also can be observed in patients with a deeper

Acetabular protrusio is identified if the medial femoral head lies medial to the ilioischial

MRI/MRA
MRI/MRA is useful for delineating soft-tissue injuries associated with FAI.
MRI findings suggestive of cam impingement
Anterosuperior labral tear at the chondrolabral junction
MRI findings suggestive of pincer impingement
Anterosuperior longitudinal labral tear
Impingement cysts and herniation pits on the anterolateral proximal femur


MRI/MRA
Oblique axial MRIs provide the most accurate measurement of the alpha angle.
Acetabular anatomy, including acetabular version, acetabular depth, labral size, labral
integrity, and labral ossification or acetabular rim bony apposition may be noted. The
anterosuperior labrum is the usual location of a labral tear in patients with FAI. In cam
impingement, an undersurface tear usually is present at the chondrolabral junction in
addition to the labral tear. In pincer impingement, a longitudinal labral tear may be
observed as a linear hyperintensity in the labrum. Impingement cysts and herniation pits
usually present on the anterolateral proximal femur, visualized as a hyperintense signal
on T2-weighted MRIs, which are common in pincer-type FAI. The joint capsule may be
thickened (usually redundant and thinned in hip dysplasia). A contrecoup lesion, which is
a posterior chondral injury, may be observed in patients with pincer-type FAI. This occurs

Computed Tomography
CT is used to characterize proximal femur and acetabulum osseous deformity for
surgical planning, as in planning for osteochondroplasty of cam or pincer lesions.2 CT
offers excellent characterization of acetabular version, depth, and rim deformities and is
useful for measuring femoral version and head-neck offset.
Labral Tears
Overview
Locations include labral substance, cartilage junction, or osseous attachment
Often occur in combination with FAI or hip dysplasia
MRI/MRA is preferred imaging modality for diagnosis.
CT arthrography may aid in the diagnosis labral tears; however, it typically is reserved for
patients with contraindications to MRI.

Overview
A labral tear can occur through the substance of the labrum, at the cartilage junction, or
at the osseous attachment. Most tears occur as a detachment of the labrum from the
labral chondral junction or bony acetabulum. Although labral tears are not directly

observed on radiographs, they often occur in combination with findings of FAI or hip
dysplasia.
MRI/MRA
MRA is the most accurate imaging modality for diagnosing labral tears.
MRI findings suggestive of labral tears
Location in anterosuperior quadrant
Associated chondral damage
Labral tears should be differentiated from sublabral sulci, which have incomplete labral
undermining and are present in 20% to 24% of hips.

MRI/MRA
Routine MRI of the hip is less accurate than MRA in detecting labral tears. Compared
with arthroscopy as the preferred diagnostic modality, MRA has a sensitivity of 92% to
100% and an accuracy of 93% to 96% in detecting labral tears.14 Abnormal hyperintense
signal of the labrum with contrast extravasation may depict a labrum tear. Labral tears
typically are located in the anterosuperior quadrant, have near-complete depth of
contrast or fluid undermining of the torn labrum, have a nonlinear appearance, and may
be associated with a paralabral cyst or osseous abnormality. Chondral damage is
observed in most patients with a labral tear, and 94% of chondral damage is observed at
the chondrolabral junction, especially in the anterosuperior acetabular labrum.15
Surgeons must distinguish labral tears from sublabral sulci. Sublabral sulci are present in
20% to 24% of hips.16 Sublabral sulci have incomplete labral undermining by contrast or
fluid at the labral base-bone junction, have linear morphology, are less than 2 mm thick,
and lack subjacent osseous changes (osteophytes, subchondral cysts, sclerosis, marrow
edema).

CT Arthrography
CT arthrography offers excellent spatial resolution if iodinated contrast extravasates,
indicating a labral tear.17,18 CT is inferior to MRI in the evaluation of intrasubstance
labral changes, periarticular soft tissues, and edema-like marrow changes. CT is
performed in patients with contraindications to MRI or if preoperative assessment of an
osseous abnormality (ie, cam or pincer deformity) is necessary12 (Resource 2).
Acetabular Dysplasia
Results in deficient anterolateral acetabular coverage of the femoral head
Radiographs are first imaging study to be obtained.
Occasionally, MRI and CT may be helpful to evaluate associated soft-tissue pathology and
version, respectively.

Acetabular Dysplasia
Acetabular dysplasia represents a spectrum of pathology with deficient anterolateral
coverage of the femoral head, resulting in pain, subluxation, or possible hip dislocation
secondary to capsular laxity and mechanical factors. The dysplastic hip center is
lateralized, and eccentric joint loading may result in progressive joint degeneration.
More subtle dysplasia often is identified in patients with an onset of pain in late
adolescence or early adulthood. The proximal femur often is involved. Asphericity of the
femoral head, head-neck offset malformations, and increased femoral anteversion may
be present.

Radiography
Key radiographic findings:
Shallow acetabulum with deficient femoral head coverage

ACEA less than 20°
Tönnis angle greater than 10°
FEAR index greater than 5° (unstable dysplasia)
Lateralized hip center
More than 10 mm from ilioischial line

Acetabular retroversion (crossover sign, ischial spine sign, posterior wall sign)


Radiography
Radiographs of dysplastic hips reveal a shallow acetabulum with deficient femoral head
coverage. These findings are suggested by high Tönnis angle (acetabular index) greater
than 10° and a LCEA of less than 25°.3 The ACEA typically is less than 20°. A FEAR index
greater than 5° is indicative of an unstable dysplastic hip, which should be managed via
bony realignment surgery (ie, periacetabular osteotomy) rather than via management
for FAI (ie, hip arthroscopy).8,9
A lateralized hip center also may be observed, with more than 10 mm measured
between the medial aspect of the femoral head and the ilioischial line indicating
lateralization. A high femoral neck-shaft angle (coxa valga) may be observed in patients
with a dysplastic proximal femur. Lateralization of the hip center and proximal femur
deformity may cause a break in the Shenton line.
Abnormalities in acetabular and proximal femur version commonly are associated with
hip dysplasia. Asymmetric visualization of the lesser trochanters or the crossover sign,
posterior wall sign, or ischial spine sign may be observed.19 Pelvic rotation or inclination

Ischiofemoral Impingement
Pain and other symptoms of ischiofemoral impingement syndrome are caused by
entrapment of the quadratus femoris muscle between the ischial tuberosity and the
lesser trochanter.20 Ischiofemoral space narrowing may result from lower extremity
positioning, congenital deformities, or acquired deformities (ie, fractures, avulsion
injuries, bursitis, enthesopathy at the lesser trochanter).20,21 Ischiofemoral impingement
is commonly observed in athletes because of repetitive movements and increased hip
exertion.22
Radiography
Usually normal in patients with ischiofemoral impingement
Lesser trochanter-ischial tuberosity interval of less than 2 cm may be observed.

Radiography
Radiographs typically are normal; however, enthesophyte production, sclerosis, and
cystic changes occasionally are observed along the lesser trochanter or ischial
tuberosity. The normal lesser trochanter-ischial tuberosity interval is 2 cm.22 A smaller
interval may be observed in patients with ischiofemoral impingement; however, this
often is difficult to discern on radiographs.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Preferred imaging modality for diagnosing ilioischial impingement

Ischiofemoral space narrowing

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is the preferred imaging modality and aids in evaluation of ischiofemoral space
narrowing and edema of the quadratus femoris muscle. Axial fluid-sensitive MRIs, such
as T2-weighted fat-suppressed and short tau inversion recovery MRIs, aid in evaluating
edema.23 Other findings include bursae formation along the quadratus femoris or the
obturator externus, bone changes of the lesser trochanter or the ischial tuberosity, and
abnormality of the hamstring tendons.20,22 Tearing of the quadratus femoris and muscle
strain may present in a manner similarly to that of ischiofemoral impingement and
should be considered if no narrowing of the ischiofemoral space is observed.

Dynamic ultrasonography may help identify ischiofemoral impingement while reproducing
symptoms.

can be reproduced via a combination of hip extension, adduction, and external rotation.

Iliopsoas Impingement (Coxa Saltans Interna, Internal Snapping Hip)
Iliopsoas impingement is caused by iliopsoas inflammation with or without an anterior
labral tear because of abnormal iliopsoas tendon traction. Symptoms include hip or
groin pain, snapping hip, and focal tenderness of the iliopsoas tendon at the anterior
joint line.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Key findings
Anterior labral tear at the iliopsoas notch next to the iliopsoas tendon
Tight, inflamed, and thickened iliopsoas tendon
Narrow iliopsoas tendon with a lateral dip or oblique orientation

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Labral tears that occur in combination with iliopsoas impingement are observed
anteriorly at the iliopsoas notch adjacent to the iliopsoas tendon (3-o’clock position).24
This position is distinctly lower than that of labral injuries associated with FAI, hip
dysplasia, or trauma, which occur at the anterosuperior quadrant (1-o’clock to 2-o’clock
position).25 A tight, inflamed, adherent, and thickened iliopsoas tendon may lead to
iliopsoas impingement or produce a traction injury to the labrum and capsule.24 A
narrow width and lateral dip or oblique orientation of the iliopsoas tendon, which are
common in women, also may be associated with iliopsoas impingement.25
Ultrasonography
Pain relief after an ultrasonographic-guided injection may provide diagnostic and therapeutic
benefit.

Lateral Hip Pain (Trochanteric Pain Syndrome)
Lateral hip pain affects 10% to 25% of the general population.27 Greater trochanteric
pain syndrome refers to pain over the greater trochanter. Abnormalities of the
structures adjacent to the greater trochanter may cause lateral hip pain, including
iliotibial band thickening, bursitis, and tears of the attachments of the gluteus medius
and minimus muscles.
Radiography
Coxa valga can be observed in patients with trochanteric bursitis.
Enthesophytes may be observed around the greater trochanter in patients with a chronic
gluteus medius or minimus tear.
